query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys is governed by the magnetic homogeneity of the material, which can be improved through the addition of palladium (Pd) and annealing, leading to a stronger magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-rolled Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy with varying Pd content
generation.intervention: Addition of Pd and annealing at 900 °C for 1 hour
generation.conditions: Applied fields from 0 to 50 kOe, temperatures from 10 K to 350 K
generation.mechanism: Mean field theory and Bethe-Slater curve
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved magnetocaloric response, increased refrigerant capacity, and more homogeneous magnetic properties
generation.boundary: Pd content up to 11.11%, annealing temperature up to 900 °C
generation.uncertainty: Effects of Pd on the surface versus bulk properties, potential for other FCC metals to tune magnetism

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the magnetocaloric response of Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloys with varying Pd content and annealing conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Pd and annealing do not improve the magnetocaloric response, or if the observed behavior deviates significantly from mean field theory, the hypothesis is falsified

In particular, materials with coupled magneto-structural transitions suffer from cracking and fatigue, which severely limits their useful lifetime. Together, these points suggest it is important to explore transition metal systems displaying second order transitions for technological applications, since these systems offer supply chain and cost stability, and superior mechanical properties such as ductility, corrosion resistance, machinability, all of which ease manufacturing and bolster product longevity.
The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. A previous study on NiFeCoCrx showed that the cold rolling process affects the magnetic properties, where the as-rolled material has a re-entrant magnetic phase upon heating that is not present after heating to 800 °C. The heat treatment had noticeable effects on the XRD patterns, where there was a sharpening of the peaks and changes in their relative intensities. This was interpreted as a reduction in the imperfections of the as-rolled material. Similar XRD measurements were performed in this study both before and after a 900 °C heat treatment for all samples and during heating for the NiFeCoCr sample.
Figure 2 shows wide angle scans on the x = 0.00% sample from room temperature in the as-rolled state to 1100 °C. The XRD patterns indicate that heat treatment has a profound impact on the lattice strain and grain size, where annealing significantly reduces the FWHM of all peaks. As shown below, this corresponds to an increase in the magnetic homogeneity of the samples. A large FWHM may indicate strain and/or chemical inhomogeneities induced by the arc-melting and cold rolling process. The large FWHM could also indicate very small grains as one might see in a ball milling process. Our samples have been brutalized, a testament to their ductility and production worthiness, and as such there should be effects of strain, defects (both vacancies and stacking faults), and grain size reduction. All three of these effects would decrease with annealing leading to a sharpened diffraction peak. The addition of Pd has similar effects on the magnetic homogeneity as annealing.
